conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states that large, high-quality randomized controlled trials consistently show hydroxychloroquine does not reduce mortality from COVID-19 and that the claim is not supported by credible evidence.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
The evidence does not support the premise. Large, high-quality randomized controlled trials consistently show hydroxychloroquine does **not** reduce mortality from COVID-19, and some analyses suggest possible harm.

The UK's RECOVERY trial, one of the largest COVID-19 treatment trials conducted, found "no significant difference in mortality rate at 28 days between those randomised to hydroxychloroquine treatment and those to usual care" (https://www.recoverytrial.net/results/hydroxychloroquine-results), a finding also reported in NEJM (https://www.nejm.org/doi/pdf/10.1056/NEJMoa2022926).

The WHO's Solidarity Trial, another major multinational RCT, reached the same conclusion: hydroxychloroquine "appeared to have little or no effect on hospitalized COVID-19, as indicated by overall mortality" (https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/coronavirus-disease-covid-19-hydroxychloroquine). The WHO explicitly states both Solidarity and RECOVERY data show hydroxychloroquine does not reduce mortality compared to standard care.

A comprehensive meta-analysis of published and unpublished randomized trials by Axfors et al., published in Nature Communications, went further, finding that hydroxychloroquine treatment was actually associated with **increased** mortality in COVID-19 patients (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-22446-z).

There is some conflicting analysis: a later reanalysis (Pasquier et al., Nature Communications, 2025) argued that after statistical adjustments, hydroxychloroquine's association with increased inpatient mortality was not statistically significant, though it still showed no mortality benefit (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-60478-x). Notably, a non-peer-reviewed aggregator site (c19early.org) claims positive effects, but this contradicts the peer-reviewed RCT evidence and lacks the rigor of RECOVERY, Solidarity, or the Axfors meta-analysis.

**Conclusion:** The weight of evidence from major randomized trials indicates hydroxychloroquine does not reduce, and may even increase, COVID-19 mortality. The premise that it reduces death is not supported by credible evidence.
